summary: Explains why circular motion requires centripetal acceleration and force even at constant speed, derives a_c = v^2/r = r*omega^2, and shows centripetal force F_c = mv^2/r = mr*omega^2 is the net result of real forces like tension, gravity, friction, or the normal force.
title: Centripetal Force and Acceleration

summary: Defines circular motion, distinguishes uniform from non-uniform circular motion, and surveys the key parameters that describe it: angular displacement, angular velocity, angular acceleration, tangential velocity, centripetal acceleration and force, and the fictitious centrifugal force.
title: Circular Motion

summary: Introduces moment of inertia as the rotational analogue of mass, its formula for a point mass and rigid bodies, radius of gyration, torque as the rotational analogue of force, and the rotational form of Newton's Second Law (tau = I*alpha).
title: Torque and Moment of Inertia

summary: Defines angular momentum both as L = r x p (cross product) and L = I*omega for a rigid body, its direction, units, and the law of conservation of angular momentum with the torque-angular-momentum relation.
title: Angular Momentum

topicTitle: 4.9 The Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum
summary: States the Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum (L is constant when net external torque is zero), derives it from tau_net = dL/dt, shows its implication I*omega = constant, applies it to skaters, divers, and star formation, compares it to linear momentum conservation, and explains why internal forces cannot change total angular momentum.
title: The Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum

summary: Defines rotational kinetic energy K.E._rot = (1/2)*I*omega^2, derives it by summing the kinetic energy of every particle in a rigid body, and applies it to rolling objects on an incline, showing a solid disc reaches the bottom faster than a hoop of the same mass and radius because the hoop has a larger moment of inertia.
title: Rotational Kinetic Energy

summary: Explains why banked roads use a component of the normal force to supply centripetal force, derives the ideal banking angle tan(theta) = v^2/(rg) by resolving the normal force, and shows the result is independent of vehicle mass.
title: 4.7 Banking of Roads

summary: Distinguishes natural from artificial satellites, derives orbital velocity v = sqrt(GM/r), surveys satellite types (communication, navigation, Earth observation, scientific) and their orbits, and explains weightlessness in orbit and artificial gravity as consequences of free fall and rotation.
title: Artificial Satellites

summary: Defines the three conditions for a geostationary orbit (24-hour period, equatorial plane, west-to-east direction), derives the orbital radius from F_g = F_c, calculates the altitude (~35,800 km) and orbital velocity (~3.07 km/s), and notes the tradeoffs of latency and launch cost.
title: 4.17 Geostationary Orbits

summary: Derives orbital velocity v = sqrt(GM/r) by setting gravitational force equal to centripetal force, shows it is independent of the orbiting object's mass and decreases with orbital radius, and explains weightlessness in orbit as continuous free fall rather than an absence of gravity.
title: Orbital Velocity

topicTitle: 4.15 Communication Satellites and Weightlessness in Orbit
summary: Covers geostationary communication satellites (orbit at ~35,786 km, 24-hour period, 3 satellites for global coverage, microwave uplink/downlink via transponders, solar power, INTELSAT) and explains why orbiting objects are weightless: the satellite is in continuous free fall, so there is no normal force between an object and its support even though gravity is still acting.
title: Communication Satellites and Weightlessness in Orbit

summary: Distinguishes mass from weight, explains apparent weight as the contact force felt during free fall (falling elevator and orbiting spacecraft), derives orbital (critical) velocity v = sqrt(g(R+h)), and shows how rotating a spacecraft produces artificial gravity via a_c = omega^2*R = g.
title: Weightlessness in Orbit

summary: Explains how rotating a spacecraft creates artificial gravity via centripetal force, derives the required angular velocity omega = sqrt(g/r) and frequency f = (1/2*pi)*sqrt(g/r), and covers practical design challenges: the size-vs-rotation-speed tradeoff, the Coriolis effect, and the gravity gradient.
title: 4.16 Artificial Gravity

summary: Distinguishes real weight (mg) from apparent weight (the normal force a scale reads), and derives the scale reading N in four elevator scenarios: at rest or constant velocity (N=mg), accelerating upward (N=m(g+a)), accelerating downward (N=m(g-a)), and free fall (N=0, weightlessness).
title: Apparent Weight in an Elevator

topicTitle: 4.19 Newton's vs. Einstein's View on Gravitation
summary: Contrasts Newton's view of gravity as an instantaneous force (F = Gm1m2/r^2) with Einstein's General Relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime, covers the experimental evidence for Einstein's theory (starlight bending, Mercury's precession, the Equivalence Principle), and explains orbital weightlessness from both perspectives.
title: Newton's vs. Einstein's View on Gravitation

summary: States the Work-Energy Principle (W_net = delta K.E.), derives it from Newton's Second Law and the third equation of motion, interprets positive/negative/zero net work, and works a numeric example calculating net work from initial and final kinetic energy.
title: 5.3 Work-Energy Principle

topicTitle: 5.2 Work Done by a Constant and Variable Force
summary: Defines work as the dot product W = Fd*cos(theta) for a constant force, covers when work is positive, negative, or zero, and explains that for a variable force (like a spring), work must be found as the area under a Force-Displacement (or Force-Extension) graph, or via the integral W = integral of F dd.
title: Work Done by a Constant and Variable Force

summary: Defines kinetic energy K.E. = (1/2)mv^2, derives it from Newton's Second Law and the equations of motion, expresses it in terms of momentum as K.E. = p^2/(2m), and states the Work-Energy Theorem W_net = delta K.E., including its form when a resistive medium removes energy as heat.
title: Introduction

summary: Defines gravitational (P.E. = mgh) and elastic ((1/2)kx^2) potential energy as stored energy due to position or deformation, and distinguishes conservative forces (path-independent, allow potential energy to be defined, e.g. gravity, springs) from non-conservative forces (path-dependent, dissipate energy, e.g. friction), explaining why mechanical energy is conserved only when non-conservative forces are absent.
title: Potential Energy (P.E.)

summary: Defines absolute gravitational potential energy U_g = -GMm/r with the zero reference at infinite distance, derives this formula via a telescoping sum of small work increments, and explains why U_g is always negative and how it relates to the mgh approximation used near Earth's surface.
title: Absolute Gravitational Potential Energy

topicTitle: 5.6 Work Done in a Gravitational Field
summary: Defines gravitational field strength g = GM/r^2, explains what makes a field conservative (path-independent work, zero work over closed paths), and proves gravity is conservative by showing the work done between two points is the same along a straight and a curved path, and zero around any closed loop.
title: Work Done in a Gravitational Field

topicTitle: 5.7 Interconversion of Kinetic and Potential Energy
summary: Explains how kinetic and potential energy convert into each other while total mechanical energy (K.E. + P.E.) stays constant under conservative forces, illustrated with a freely falling object (v = sqrt(2gh)) and a swinging pendulum, and shows how friction breaks the conservation by converting some energy into heat.
title: Interconversion of Kinetic and Potential Energy

topicTitle: 5.8 Work-Energy Principle in a Resistive Medium
summary: Extends the Work-Energy Principle to include resistive forces (friction, air resistance), which always do negative work (W_resistive = -F*d), showing W_net = W_applied + W_resistive = delta K.E., derives mgh = (1/2)mv^2 + fh for a body falling through resistance, and solves a numeric example combining applied force and friction.
title: Work-Energy Principle in a Resistive Medium

summary: Defines power P = W/t as the rate of doing work, covers its units (watt, kilowatt, horsepower), distinguishes average from instantaneous power, derives P = F.v, and clarifies that the kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy (3.6 x 10^6 J), not power.
title: Power

summary: Defines efficiency as the ratio of useful output to total input energy or power, explains why real machines are always below 100% efficiency, and covers the Carnot engine's theoretical maximum efficiency eta = 1 - T_sink/T_source, worked with the freezing/boiling point example (~26.8%).
title: 5.5 Efficiency

summary: Defines escape velocity as the minimum speed to break free from a planet's gravity, derives v_esc = sqrt(2GM/R) from energy conservation (total mechanical energy = 0), gives the equivalent form v_esc = sqrt(2gR) using surface gravity, and calculates Earth's escape velocity as approximately 11.2 km/s.
title: Escape Velocity

summary: Surveys five non-conventional (renewable) energy sources: tidal energy (dams harnessing tidal rise/fall), wave energy (devices like Salter's Duck), solar energy (thermal collectors and photovoltaic cells), geothermal energy (heat from hot springs, geysers, and hot rocks), and biomass (stored solar energy in organic matter).
title: Non-Conventional Energy Sources

summary: Defines biomass as stored solar energy in organic matter and covers the three main conversion methods: direct combustion (burning for heat/steam), fermentation (producing ethanol biofuel), and biogas production (anaerobic digestion yielding methane biogas and fertilizer slurry).
title: Biomass Energy

summary: Explains geothermal energy as heat from radioactive decay, residual planetary heat, and compression, covers how it is harnessed via natural manifestations (hot springs, geysers, fumaroles), electricity generation as a heat engine (W = Q_H - Q_C), and Hot Dry Rock direct heating, and discusses energy degradation and environmental impact on geysers.
title: Geothermal Energy

summary: Explains buoyant force (upthrust) as the pressure difference between the top and bottom of a submerged object, derives Archimedes' Principle F_B = rho_f*V_sub*g, covers the Principle of Flotation (sink/float/suspend conditions), and applies these ideas to ships, submarines, and hot-air balloons.
title: Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy

summary: Distinguishes streamline (laminar) flow, smooth and predictable, from turbulent flow, chaotic with eddies, defines the theoretical ideal fluid (non-viscous, incompressible, steady, irrotational), and explains why real fluids are viscous due to internal friction between layers.
title: Types of Fluid Flow

summary: Derives the Equation of Continuity from conservation of mass: rho_1*A_1*v_1 = rho_2*A_2*v_2 for real fluids, simplifying to A_1*v_1 = A_2*v_2 for an ideal incompressible fluid, showing fluid speeds up where a pipe narrows and slows where it widens.
title: 6.3 Equation of Continuity

summary: States Bernoulli's Equation P + (1/2)*rho*v^2 + rho*g*h = constant as conservation of energy for an ideal fluid, derives it from the work-energy theorem applied to pressure forces on a moving fluid segment, and notes its limitation to ideal (non-viscous, incompressible) fluids in steady streamline flow.
title: Bernoulli's Equation

summary: Surveys seven practical applications of Bernoulli's Equation: speed of efflux (Torricelli's Theorem), the Venturi effect and meter, filter pumps, atomizers, lift on an aerofoil, the swing of a spinning ball, and blood flow through constricted arteries.
title: Applications of Bernoulli's Equation

summary: States Torricelli's Theorem, v = sqrt(2gh), the speed of efflux from a hole at depth h equals the speed of free fall from that height, and derives it from Bernoulli's Equation using the assumptions of equal atmospheric pressure at both points and a negligible fall speed at the reservoir's top surface.
title: 6.4.2 Torricelli's Theorem

summary: Explains how a Venturi meter measures flow rate by narrowing a pipe (converging section, throat, diverging section) to trade velocity for pressure, and derives the inlet velocity formula V_1 = A_2*sqrt(2gh)/sqrt(A_1^2-A_2^2) by combining Bernoulli's equation with the equation of continuity.
title: Venturi Meter

summary: Explains how an aerofoil generates lift via Bernoulli's principle (F_L = (P_1-P_2)*A) and Newton's third law, covers angle of attack and stalling, and extends the same pressure-difference idea to the Magnus effect that curves a spinning cricket ball.
title: Aerofoil

summary: Defines viscosity (coefficient eta, Pa.s, dimensions ML^-1T^-1) and drag force, states Stokes' Law F_d = 6*pi*eta*r*v for small spheres at low speed, and derives terminal velocity v_t = 2r^2(rho_s-rho_f)g / (9*eta), showing it scales with r^2.
title: Viscosity and Drag

summary: Covers fluid friction (drag) broadly: viscosity's role in generating drag, the general high-velocity drag equation F_D = (1/2)*rho*v^2*C_D*A versus Stokes' Law F=6*pi*eta*r*v for small spheres at low speed, terminal velocity as the force-balance condition, and a real-world streamlining example.
title: Fluid Friction and Drag

summary: Defines terminal velocity as the point where gravitational force balances drag force (net force and acceleration both zero), derives v_t = 2*rho*g*r^2/(9*eta) for a falling sphere using Stokes' Law, and applies the idea to a paratrooper's two-phase jump and everyday conceptual questions about falling objects.
title: Terminal Velocity

summary: Explains superfluidity as zero-viscosity flow (seen below the Lambda Point in Helium-4 and Helium-3), its defining characteristics (persistent motion, high thermal conductivity, quantum coherence), quantized vortex formation under rotation, and real-world applications from gyroscopes to MRI coolants.
title: Superfluidity

summary: Classifies solids by internal atomic structure into crystalline (ordered lattice, anisotropic, sharp melting point), polycrystalline (many randomly-oriented grains, isotropic), and amorphous (no long-range order, isotropic, softens gradually), and introduces the unit cell as the smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice (simple cubic, BCC, FCC).
title: 7.1 Classification of Solids

summary: Covers tensile/compressive deformation, defines stress (sigma=F/A) and strain (dimensionless), the three moduli of elasticity (Young's, Shear, Bulk), the stress-vs-pressure distinction, elastic vs plastic deformation, and elastic potential energy U = (1/2)*F*deltaL stored during elastic deformation.
title: Deformation in Solids

summary: Defines elastic potential energy as the work done to deform a material elastically, derives it as the area under the force-extension graph (W = (1/2)*F*x = (1/2)*k*x^2), and generalizes it to strain energy density = (1/2)*stress*strain.
title: Elastic Potential Energy

summary: States the First Law of Thermodynamics (Q = deltaU + W) as conservation of energy applied to heat, internal energy, and work, gives real-world examples, and surveys the four special-case thermodynamic processes (isothermal, adiabatic, isochoric, isobaric) each derived from the general equation.
title: First Law of Thermodynamics

summary: Covers the Second Law of Thermodynamics: heat engine efficiency, the Kelvin-Planck (no 100%-efficient heat engine) and Clausius (heat doesn't spontaneously flow cold to hot) statements, reversible vs irreversible processes, entropy as a measure of disorder (deltaS = Q/T, always increasing for real processes), and energy degradation from high-quality to low-quality (waste heat) forms.
title: Second Law of Thermodynamics

summary: Defines an adiabatic process (Q=0) and derives PV^gamma = constant by combining the First Law with the Ideal Gas Law, introduces the adiabatic index gamma = Cp/Cv, gives the T-V and T-P adiabatic relations, and compares the adiabatic curve (steeper, since gamma>1) with the isothermal curve on a P-V diagram.
title: Adiabatic Process and Equation

topicTitle: 8.4 Applications of the First Law of Thermodynamics
summary: Applies the First Law (Q = deltaU + W) to the four special-case processes: isochoric (W=0, Q=deltaU), isobaric (Q=deltaU+PdeltaV), isothermal (deltaU=0, Q=W), and adiabatic (Q=0, deltaU=-W), comparing their PV-diagram shapes and contrasting adiabatic vs isothermal expansion from the same starting point.
title: Applications of the First Law of Thermodynamics

topicTitle: 8.5 Carnot Heat Engine and Carnot Cycle
summary: Describes the idealized Carnot heat engine and its 4-step reversible cycle (isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression) between hot reservoir T1 and cold reservoir T2, derives the efficiency formula E = 1 - T2/T1, and states Carnot's theorem that no engine between the same two temperatures can exceed this efficiency.
title: Carnot Heat Engine and Carnot Cycle

summary: Defines entropy as a measure of disorder (deltaS = deltaQ_rev/T, J/K, a state function), explains how temperature and irreversibility increase it (deltaS_total >= 0), covers the tendency of isolated systems toward disorder, energy degradation, applications in heat-engine efficiency limits and the ideal-gas entropy formula, and the hypothetical heat death of the universe.
title: Entropy

summary: Defines a heat engine (hot reservoir, working substance, cold reservoir) and its efficiency eta = W/Qh = 1 - Qc/Qh, applies it to the petrol engine's four-stroke cycle (25-30% efficient), and introduces the Carnot engine as the theoretical efficiency ceiling eta_Carnot = 1 - Tc/Th.
title: Heat Engine

summary: Explains gas pressure and temperature from molecular motion (P=(1/3)*rho*<v^2>, <K.E.>=(3/2)*kB*T, v_rms=sqrt(3RT/M)) under the kinetic theory's assumptions, states the Ideal Gas Law PV=nRT, and covers work done by/on a gas (W=P*deltaV) as the area under a P-V curve.
title: Kinetic Theory of Gases

summary: Reviews heat capacity and specific heat, then defines the molar specific heats of a gas at constant volume (Cv: nCv*deltaT = deltaU) and constant pressure (Cp: nCp*deltaT = deltaU + P*deltaV), explains why Cp > Cv, and derives Mayer's relation Cp - Cv = R.
title: Molar Specific Heats $C_p$ and $C_v$

summary: Describes the Carnot refrigerator as a Carnot engine run in reverse (a reversed 4-step cycle) that uses work input to move heat from a cold reservoir to a hot one (QH = QL + W), defines the Coefficient of Performance COP = QL/W = TL/(TH-TL), and distinguishes a refrigerator (desired effect QL) from a heat pump (desired effect QH).
title: The Carnot Refrigerator

topicTitle: 8.11 Thermodynamic Processes: Reversible, Irreversible, and Cyclic
summary: Distinguishes reversible processes (idealized, quasi-static, no dissipation, zero net entropy change), irreversible processes (all real natural processes, entropy always increases), and cyclic processes (return to the initial state, so deltaU_cycle=0 and Q=W), and explains why reversible processes remain a useful theoretical benchmark despite never occurring in reality.
title: Thermodynamic Processes: Reversible, Irreversible, and Cyclic

summary: Covers the three experimental gas laws relating P, V, T for a fixed amount of gas: Boyle's Law (PV=constant at fixed T), Charles's Law (V/T=constant at fixed P), and Gay-Lussac's Law (P/T=constant at fixed V), then combines them into the Ideal Gas Equation PV=nRT.
title: The Gas Laws

summary: Explains the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics and thermal equilibrium (no net heat flow, same temperature), defines internal energy as the sum of molecular kinetic and potential energies (for an ideal gas, average KE per molecule = (3/2)*k*T, so U depends only on T), and restates the Ideal Gas Law PV=nRT=NkT.
title: Thermal Equilibrium and Internal Energy

summary: States the Principle of Superposition (y = y1+y2+...+yn) and shows how it produces three distinct effects depending on the interacting waves: interference (same frequency, same direction), stationary waves (same frequency/amplitude, opposite directions), and beats (slightly different frequencies, same direction), then defines coherent waves as the condition needed for stable interference.
title: 9.2 Superposition of Waves

summary: Defines interference via the principle of superposition, distinguishes constructive interference (path difference = m*lambda, max amplitude) from destructive interference (path difference = (m+1/2)*lambda, min amplitude), and explains why observable interference requires coherent sources, illustrated by why car headlights don't interfere.
title: Interference of Waves

summary: Explains beats as the periodic loudness variation heard when two slightly-different-frequency sound waves interfere, gives the beat frequency formula f_beat = |f1-f2|, the human ear's roughly 10 Hz perception limit, and applications in tuning instruments and determining an unknown frequency (e.g. loading a tuning fork with wax).
title: Beats

summary: Explains stationary waves as the superposition of two identical progressive waves traveling in opposite directions (y = 2A*sin(kx)*cos(wt)), defines nodes and antinodes and their spacing (lambda/4 apart), derives the harmonic series for a string fixed at both ends (f_n = n*f_1), and contrasts progressive vs stationary waves.
title: 9.3 Stationary Waves

summary: Covers longitudinal stationary waves in organ pipes: a closed-end pipe (node at closed end, antinode at open end) supports only odd harmonics with f1=v/4L, an open-end pipe (antinode at both ends) supports all harmonics with f1=v/2L, and end correction accounts for the antinode forming slightly outside the open end.
title: 9.3.2 Stationary Waves in Air Column

summary: Describes the resonance-tube experiment for demonstrating stationary waves in an air column (tuning fork over an adjustable water-level tube), explains resonance and node/antinode boundary conditions, derives the odd-harmonic resonance lengths (lambda/4, 3lambda/4, ...), and shows how measuring successive resonance lengths gives the speed of sound v = f*2*(L2-L1).
title: Experimental Setup and Procedure

summary: Explains resonance in an air column as large-amplitude vibration when a driving frequency matches a natural frequency, links it to stationary-wave formation, distinguishes transverse from longitudinal waves, contrasts closed-pipe (odd harmonics, f_n=n*v/4L) versus open-pipe (all harmonics, f_n=n*v/2L) resonance, and covers end correction and the harmonic-vs-overtone distinction.
title: Resonance of an Air Column

summary: Explains diffraction as waves bending around obstacles/apertures via Huygens' Principle, most noticeable when the obstacle/slit size is comparable to the wavelength, illustrated with water waves, single-slit light diffraction, diffraction gratings (d*sin(theta)=n*lambda), X-ray diffraction (Bragg's Law), why sound diffracts around corners but light doesn't, and how diffraction differs from interference.
title: Diffraction of Waves

summary: Explains polarization as a property unique to transverse waves, covers polarization by Polaroid filters (Malus's Law I=I0*cos^2(theta)) and by reflection (Brewster's Law n=tan(ip)), and surveys applications in photography, stress analysis, 3D movies, and optical activity.
title: 9.8 Polarization

summary: Defines wave intensity I = P/A (W/m^2), and covers the three factors affecting it: intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, proportional to the duration of exposure (total energy), and inversely proportional to the square of the distance from a point source (I is proportional to 1/r^2).
title: 9.1 Intensity of Waves

topicTitle: 9.11 Speed of Sound: Newton's Formula and Laplace's Correction
summary: Derives the speed of sound V=sqrt(E/rho): Newton's isothermal assumption gives V=sqrt(P/rho) (~280 m/s, 16% too low), and Laplace's correction, recognizing sound propagation as adiabatic, gives V=sqrt(gamma*P/rho) (~332 m/s), matching the measured value.
title: Speed of Sound: Newton's Formula and Laplace's Correction

topicTitle: 9.12 Factors Affecting the Speed of Sound
summary: Analyzes how density, pressure, moisture, wind, and temperature affect the speed of sound: V = sqrt(gamma*P/rho) decreases with density, is unaffected by pressure alone at constant temperature, increases with moisture (lower density), shifts by wind speed, and increases by about 0.61 m/s per 1C rise in temperature.
title: Factors Affecting the Speed of Sound

summary: Covers the Doppler Effect (apparent frequency shift from relative source/observer motion) via the general formula f' = f*(v+-v_o)/(v-+v_s), works through all 6 motion cases (observer/source moving toward or away, singly or combined), and surveys applications in radar, sonar, medical ultrasound, and astronomical red/blue shift.
title: The Doppler Effect

summary: Surveys real-world applications of the Doppler Effect: radar and SONAR for speed/location detection, astronomical red/blue shift for the expanding universe and exoplanet detection, medical Doppler ultrasound for blood flow imaging, Doppler weather radar for storm tracking, and satellite navigation/tracking.
title: Applications of the Doppler Effect

summary: Explains gravitational waves as ripples in spacetime predicted by Einstein's General Relativity (1916), generated by accelerating massive objects like merging black holes, travel at the speed of light causing quadrupolar spacetime distortion, and are detected via laser interferometers like LIGO (first detection 2015).
title: Gravitational Waves

summary: States Coulomb's Law F=k*|q1*q2|/r^2 (k=1/(4*pi*epsilon0)), its vector form confirming mutual Newton's-third-law forces, the like/unlike-charge repel/attract rule, its inverse-square similarity to (but key differences from) gravity, the superposition principle for multiple charges, the reduction of force by a dielectric medium, and its exact validity for spherical conductors treated as point charges.
title: Coulomb's Law

summary: Defines the electric field as the region where a charge exerts force on other charges, defines electric field intensity E = F/q (a vector pointing away from positive and toward negative source charges), derives E = kQ/r^2 for a point charge from Coulomb's Law, gives its SI unit N/C (equivalent to V/m), and works a numeric example.
title: Electric Field Intensity

summary: Defines electric field lines as curves whose tangent gives the field direction, states the drawing rules (originate on positive/terminate on negative charges, never intersect, density shows field strength), and surveys common patterns (dipole, like charges with a neutral point, uniform field between parallel plates).
title: Electric Field Lines

summary: Defines a ferrofluid as a colloidal suspension of ~10 nm magnetite nanoparticles coated with surfactant in a carrier liquid, explains superparamagnetic behavior (magnetized only in an applied field, no permanent magnetism) and the surface-spiking pattern from the balance of magnetic force, gravity, and surface tension, and surveys applications: loudspeaker cooling, rotating shaft seals, targeted drug delivery, MRI contrast, and field visualization.
title: 10.4 Ferrofluid

summary: Defines potential gradient as the rate of change of electric potential with distance, states E = -dV/dr (field points toward decreasing potential), derives it from work done on a test charge, gives its unit V/m (equivalent to N/C), offers the hill-slope analogy, explains how positive/negative charges move relative to potential in a uniform field, and works a numeric point-charge distance calculation.
title: Potential Gradient

summary: Defines drift velocity as the slow, directed average velocity of charge carriers superimposed on their fast random thermal motion, contrasts it with the much larger Fermi velocity, states I = nAv_d*e, defines mobility mu = v_d/E, and works a numeric drift-velocity calculation for a copper wire, closing with why bulbs light instantly despite slow drift.
title: Drift Velocity

summary: Defines electric potential V = W/q as work per unit charge, distinguishes it from electric potential energy, gives V = kQ/r for a point charge and superposition for multiple charges, defines potential difference deltaV, relates E = -deltaV/deltaR, covers equipotential surfaces (zero work, perpendicular to field lines), the electron-volt as an energy unit, and works three numeric examples.
title: Electric Potential

topicTitle: 11.3 Electromotive Force and Maximum Power Output
summary: Defines emf as energy per unit charge from a source (e = W/q), distinguishes it from terminal voltage via VT = e - Ir (discharging) or VT = e + Ir (charging), derives circuit current I = e/(R+r), covers power dissipation/efficiency (eta = R/(R+r)), and derives the maximum power transfer condition R = r giving Pmax = e^2/(4r) at 50% efficiency.
title: Electromotive Force (emf)

summary: Explains how resistance changes with temperature via the temperature coefficient of resistance alpha (R_T = R_0[1 + alpha(T-T0)]), contrasts positive-alpha metals with negative-alpha semiconductors/insulators/electrolytes, defines resistivity R = rho*L/A and conductivity sigma = 1/rho, and covers the special cases of superconductors (zero resistance) and thermistors.
title: Variation of Resistance with Temperature

summary: Defines an LDR (photoresistor) as a component whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases via photoconductivity, contrasts intrinsic (Si/Ge) vs extrinsic (doped, e.g. CdS) types, explains the photon-absorption mechanism freeing charge carriers, lists key characteristics, covers its use in a potential-divider circuit (V_out = V_in * R_fixed/(R_LDR+R_fixed)), and surveys applications like automatic street lighting and security systems.
title: Light-Dependent Resistor (LDR)

summary: Defines electric power P = E/t = VI, derives the equivalent forms P = I^2R and P = V^2/R, explains Joule heating (energy dissipated E = Pt = I^2Rt), gives the SI unit Watt and the commercial energy unit kWh (1 kWh = 3.6x10^6 J), and works a monthly electricity-cost example.
title: Electric Power

summary: States Kirchhoff's two laws for analyzing multi-loop circuits: KCL (sum of currents at a junction = 0, from charge conservation) and KVL (sum of potential changes around a closed loop = 0, from energy conservation), gives sign conventions for KVL, and shows how both laws derive the familiar series and parallel resistor combination rules.
title: Kirchhoff's Laws

summary: Explains the null method (balancing an unknown quantity against a known standard until a detector reads zero, making measurement independent of detector calibration), covers the Wheatstone Bridge (balance condition P/Q = R/S, giving R = S(P/Q)) and the Potentiometer (comparing EMFs via balancing lengths e1/e2 = l1/l2, and finding internal resistance r = R(l1-l2)/l2).
title: The Null Method of Measurement

summary: Defines a thermistor as a heat-sensitive resistor made from sintered semiconducting metal oxides, contrasts NTC (resistance decreases with temperature, used for sensing) and PTC (resistance increases, used for self-regulating heaters/fuses) types, explains their non-linear resistance-temperature relationship (requiring calibration or the Steinhart-Hart equation), why their high temperature coefficient makes them more sensitive than metallic resistors, and surveys applications including potential-divider temperature sensing.
title: Thermistor

summary: Explains carbon fibre-reinforced concrete: embedding carbon fibres boosts tensile strength, corrosion resistance, and crack control versus plain concrete or steel rebar, at an optimal ~0.3% by volume for bridge flexural strength, and describes how the fibres' electrical conductivity enables non-destructive crack detection via resistance monitoring.
title: 11.8 Carbon Fibre in Concrete Bridge

summary: Introduces magnetic fields: sources (permanent magnets, currents, moving charges, changing E-fields), visualization via field lines (out of N, into S, closed loops, never cross, density shows strength), the field of a current-carrying wire via the right-hand grip rule, and the Lorentz force on a moving charge F = q(v x B), including the zero-force parallel case and the circular-path perpendicular case.
title: Magnetic Fields

topicTitle: 12.2 Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor

topicTitle: 12.4 Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge
